implementation_notes: Scala's standard library provides the instance for the collection types (List, Set, String, Option, Array) and collections has cats-free Semigroup/Monoid-like instances via the collection hierarchy, so most cases need no code. The generic combinator-library answer is cats' Monoid with Semigroup separated (a Monoid is a Semigroup plus an empty), which is the right modelling for types that have a combine but no natural identity - NonEmptyList is the canonical example, and its concat is associative while it has no empty. In Scala 3 the extension-method form 'given Monoid[Money] with ...' makes the instance visible at the use site.
idiom_name: Monoid/Semigroup instances; given/extends instance resolution; Option's Semigroup
pitfalls: Monoid[Boolean] is disjunction (any) and Monoid[List[A]] is concatenation - both surprising, both easy to reach for by accident in a reduce.
Requiring a Monoid for a type that has a combine but no natural empty is the moment to use Semigroup; inventing an empty (a zero-length NonEmptyList) leaks an artefact.
Combining large Lists with ++ copies the left operand each time; foldLeft into a mutable builder is linear and still associative in its result.
A given instance in implicit scope can be shadowed by a local one, changing the aggregation semantics without any visible change at the use site.
